sentences.text: In a feasibility study, researchers tested a spherical ultrasound device with a 17.5-mm radius on silicone models of brain tumor cavities filled with phosphate-buffered saline or 1% albumin to measure the visibility of markers at depths of about 3 and 5 centimeters.

The device remained stable and allowed visualization of cavity edges in all model shapes, with markers visible at 5 centimeters regardless of the fluid, although target depth had a larger effect on image clarity than fluid type.
CT scans confirmed the correct shape of the models and proper device fit, supporting the finding that the spherical device creates a consistent surface for imaging simulated cavities.
The authors conclude that testing in living subjects is necessary to determine whether the device is useful in real clinical settings.
